Hello everyone, welcome to the Electrical Expert Forum segment. I’m George Fan. Today we’ll be discussing debugging issues related to fire alarm systems.

Here’s the agenda for today’s lecture: First, we’ll review the installation, testing, inspection and verification of Fire Alarm Systems.

I briefly covered this content in a lecture a year ago. Since these topics are related to the Fire Alarm System commissioning, I will briefly review them today.

Next, I will discuss when the Fire Alarm System commissioning is required and the codes and standards applicable during the process. Additionally, I will cover the scope of work involved in such commissioning projects and the technical documents that need to be submitted. I will also explain the input information required when preparing these technical documents.

Before debugging, the Fire Alarm System must be fully or mostly installed. The programming of this system also needs to be completed. In addition, the As-built Drawings, Shop Drawings, and O&M Package should also be largely ready.

Fire Alarm Testing and Inspection is part of the Fire Alarm System commissioning. Whether it’s a new project or a TI project, Verification must be conducted. Verification must be performed by a third party, not the installers. The Verification Report needs to be submitted to the Engineer/Client for review and approval, and there should generally be no Deficiency.

Testing and Inspection are previously mentioned, while Verification is another critical component. Generally speaking, Fire Alarm Verification is a mandatory step for every project upon completion, whether it’s a new or existing project. Inspection is typically conducted annually. Verification must be performed in accordance with the ULC-537 standard and applies to all projects. Additionally, Verification must be completed and signed off by a third-party Technician.

Verification usually takes place after construction is finished and requires the completion of legal documentation based on the ULC-537 template. Once done, a Verification Report must be filled out and reviewed and approved by both the Engineer and the Commissioning Agent.

During the commissioning process of a Fire Alarm system, Fire Alarm Verification is an essential step. Unlike the commissioning of other Building Systems or equipment, the commissioning of a Fire Alarm System focuses specifically on the Fire Alarm system itself. Since the Fire Alarm system involves fire alarm functionality, it requires coordination and interfacing with many other Building systems, thus also involving the commissioning of other Building Equipment and Systems.

This is the annual inspection of the fire alarm system. It must be conducted once a year after installation or upgrade completion. This task is not closely related to commissioning, so only a brief review and information explanation are provided here.

When is commissioning of a fire alarm system required? Typically, especially for small to medium-sized projects, we do not conduct dedicated commissioning for fire alarm systems, as general projects only need to complete system verification. However, government projects, regardless of scale, require commissioning.

Commissioning is essentially a series of documentation tasks that involve participation during the design phase, verification testing during the commissioning phase, and final preparation of relevant technical documents at project closeout.

For large government projects, it is usually required to involve a third-party commissioning agent. It is important to note that all fire alarm system projects must complete verification, as this is a mandatory requirement of the code. Commissioning, however, is not a code-mandated item, though federal government projects often treat it as a compulsory requirement.

For federal government projects, it is necessary to comply with two PSPC documents, namely the PSPC Commissioning Manual and the PSPC Commissioning Guidelines.

For electrical systems, the CAN/ULC S1001-11 standard must also be followed, which covers integrated testing of fire and life safety systems as well as fire commissioning. This is the Canadian standard for life safety system testing.

For electrical systems, the CAN/ULC S1001-11 standard must also be followed, which covers integrated testing of fire and life safety systems as well as fire commissioning. This is the Canadian standard for life safety system testing.

Additionally, URC537 is another applicable specification for fire alarm system commissioning.

This section covers the scope of fire alarm system commissioning and deliverables. In the first two lectures on building commissioning overview, we have already discussed the commissioning scope and deliverables. Here we will only provide a brief review to ensure the completeness of the lecture content.

During the design phase, as the commissioning consultant, we need to review the design documents from the consulting firm, including the BOD (Basis of Design) and the sequence of operations description for the fire alarm system design, and participate in design meetings. At the same time, we also need to prepare the commissioning plan, commissioning specifications, and relevant test procedures.

Additionally, three types of checklists need to be prepared:
1. Installation startup checklist
2. Performance verification checklist
3. Integrated system test procedure

Among these, the performance verification and integrated system test procedures are closely related to the sequence of operations description for the fire alarm system. These documents are primarily developed based on the sequence of operations description.

During the construction phase, as the commissioning agent, we need to review the construction drawings of the fire alarm system. Additionally, based on the approved construction drawings and the consultant’s IFC design package, we are also required to review the commissioning plan and test procedures. Furthermore, we will attend construction meetings and promptly respond to RFI issues related to commissioning.

During the debugging phase, our workload is relatively heavy. First, we need to organize debugging meetings and prepare meeting minutes, while also guiding and supervising all debugging-related activities. Additionally, coordination with various project stakeholders is required, including workflows, scheduling, and mutual collaboration.

Upon entering the substantive debugging stage, we will proceed step-by-step according to the test checklist. The first step involves installation and startup checks, the second step is performance verification, and the final step entails executing the integrated system testing process—comprehensive debugging and validation of the entire system.

In addition to the above, we also need to review the Fire Alarm System Verification Report, prepare the Commissioning Report and Commissioning Issues Log.

Furthermore, we need to organize and participate in Training Meetings, and prepare the instruments and tools required for the testing and commissioning phase. Typically, these devices are provided by the contractor or testing company, but as the commissioning party, it is advisable to bring your own to the site for contingencies.

During the project closeout phase, as the commissioning agent, we need to complete the following tasks:

During the project closeout phase, as the commissioning agent, we need to complete the following tasks:

Review the contractor’s Operation and Maintenance (O&M) Manual and prepare the final commissioning report, which should include:

Results of the entire commissioning process

Completed work

Outstanding items

Corrective actions (action to fix deficiency) or issue log

Compile the final commissioning manual, containing:

Commissioning report

Design basis

Project requirements

Commissioning specifications

Commissioning test forms

Commissioning meeting minutes

Construction drawing review records

Commissioning issue log

Commissioning completion letter, etc.

While specific requirements may vary across projects or companies, the above content is primarily based on the federal government’s BGIS standards for commissioning. Adjustments may be made per project or client needs, but the fundamental framework remains consistent.

To complete these commissioning documents, we require the following information:

During the design phase, the client needs to provide project requirements, commissioning requirements, and relevant school requirements. We need to review applicable commissioning codes and standards and obtain the consultant’s design package, including basis of design documents, interface test documents, construction drawings, and as-built drawings.

During the construction phase, after the contractor submits shop drawings, approved shop drawings must be provided. Additionally, after the testing company completes fire alarm system commissioning, they must submit verification reports from contractors, as well as operation and maintenance manuals.

When testing and commissioning a Fire Alarm System, various instruments and tools are required. As a fire alarm system verification technician, you must carry a pre-programmed laptop and basic tools such as a multimeter and screwdriver. Additionally, the following four testing instruments are essential:

Smoke generator: Used to test smoke detectors, including ceiling-mounted and duct-mounted smoke detectors, as well as the smoke detection system in VESTA special systems.

Heat generator: Used to evaluate the performance of heat detectors.

Lux meter: For example, the Dr Meter Digital Lux Meter LX1330B, used to measure the illumination level of strobe lights in audible/visual alarms.

Sound level meter: For example, the HTI Digital Sound Level Meter HT-8OA, used to test the sound intensity of alarms (such as buzzers or sirens).

These instruments are critical during the commissioning process of a fire alarm system.

These instruments are critical during the commissioning process of a fire alarm system.

The device on the left is the smoke generator, equipped with a button at the bottom. When pressed, smoke will be discharged from the top. During testing, place a sealed smoke detector over the upper opening, then press the button to generate smoke, simulating a smoke environment and checking whether the detector triggers an alarm signal.

The testing procedure for the DACT smoke detector will be explained in detail later, as its operation is relatively more complex.

The illustration on the right shows the heat generator, used to test the performance of heat detectors. A button is located at the bottom of the device—when activated, the internal heating wire will generate heat. For testing, cover the heat detector with the lid and press the button to initiate the heating function, verifying the detector’s operational status through the produced heat.

This is an illumination test meter, which is a sensor. When activated, this sensor can measure light intensity.

On the right is a sound level tester/sound level meter, which can detect the ambient sound level (in decibels, dB) after being turned on.

We use this equipment to test the performance of fire alarm horns or fire alarm bells, as well as strobes.

Next, we will discuss the testing procedures in detail. For each individual fire alarm device, we can explain them one by one. Previously, we have introduced the smoke detectors, heat detectors, and audible/visual alarms. As for the manual call points, the testing method is relatively simple: just pull down the button cover to complete the test. After the operation, observe whether the fire alarm control panel generates the corresponding fire alarm signal.

There are actually two methods, one of which is to simulate smoke signals without using a smoke generator. Each dark smoke detector is equipped with a testing device. When the switch is in the normal position, the device operates normally; when switched to the test position, it only tests whether the electrical signal can return to the fire alarm control panel. This test does not involve the actual smoke detection function. A real test must be conducted through the small hole next to it.

For example, this is a smoke detector, specifically a dark smoke detector. After opening the red casing, you can see a small hole. Use a smoke generator to direct smoke into this hole.

The white component inside the detector is the dark smoke sensor. When the smoke concentration reaches the threshold, the detector sends a fire signal to the fire alarm control panel. Due to the small aperture, achieving the triggering concentration during debugging is often challenging. Especially when the system is running, the high airflow makes it even harder to trigger the alarm.

Therefore, during debugging, it is usually necessary to shut down the air handler and then use the smoke generator to inject smoke directly into the hole, ensuring the detector sends a signal to the control panel. This is our standard operating procedure. Next, we will proceed with other topics.

Another type is the beam smoke detector, which is primarily used in large open spaces such as warehouses. Its working principle involves achieving wide-area coverage through a transmitter and reflector, typically covering an area of approximately 200 feet in length and 60 feet in width. As shown in the diagram, these detectors are usually installed below the ceiling. The beam smoke detector emits a signal from the emitter, which is received by the reflector on the opposite side. The detector is equipped with a controller, and for simplex products, one controller can connect to two detectors. These detectors are wired to the fire alarm control panel. The reflector is positioned parallel to and opposite the emitter.

This device employs a reflector as its core component, which is fundamentally an optical reflection device rather than an electrical component. The reflector’s coverage spans approximately 60 feet. When signals emitted by the emitter (emeter) fail to return from the reflector, the system triggers a trouble signal; if the emitter continuously sends signals and receives reflected signals in return, the beam smoke detector will interpret this as a fire condition.

The debugging procedure is as follows: Use an occlusion plate to cover the reflector, and two distinct signals will be generated based on the duration of coverage:

Trouble Signal Test: Cover for 2-3 seconds, and the system will send a trouble signal to the fire alarm control panel.

Fire Alarm Test: Cover continuously for over 5 seconds, and the beam smoke detector will transmit a fire alarm signal to the fire alarm control panel.

This is a Beam Smoke Detector, and there is also a system called the VESTA Smoke Detection System. These devices are primarily used in archives.

In archives, the shelves are densely arranged with only narrow aisles in between, just enough for personnel to pass through. If traditional spot-type smoke detectors were installed at each location, the quantity would be excessive. The VESTA Smoke Detection System effectively addresses this issue.

As shown in the image, this is the controller of the system.

This is the power supply and relay. The controller can be connected to a computer to receive smoke detection signals. The signals are transmitted through pipes to different locations in the archives room, similar to a sprinkler system, detecting smoke concentration between shelves via probes or holes.

When the signal value reaches a certain threshold, the controller generates two types of signals: an alarm signal for low concentration and a fire alarm signal for high concentration. The fire alarm signal is connected to the relay, which then transmits it to the fire alarm control panel.

Below the red conduit in the diagram are the power supply and battery, providing backup power for the system.

This is the controller, this is the battery, this is the relay, and there are also some advertisements and photos. Next, we’ll continue with the explanation.

As you can see, this is the controller, this is the battery, this is the relay, and there are also some advertisements and photos. Next, we’ll continue with the explanation.

Let’s discuss the flow switch, pressure switch, and control valve temperature switch. The control valve temperature switch itself should have corresponding interfaces. As for the flow switch, how do we handle it?

Flow Switch  
From an electrical perspective, flow switches are primarily divided into two types. The first type typically has an appearance as shown in the diagram. During operation, screws must be removed to open the outer cover. The flow switch sends a signal back to the fire alarm control panel via the fire alarm monitoring module (i.e., relay), triggering a trouble alarm to indicate unauthorized opening of the device. Additionally, a jumper can be used to simulate an activation signal: since this switch uses normally open contacts, forcibly closing the contacts can simulate the activation signal of a water flow indicator. In this case, the fire alarm control panel will receive a fire alarm signal.

In practice, it is ideal if water flow is present in the pipeline, but simulating water flow is often difficult. If the sprinkler system is not activated, forcibly simulating water flow may cause severe damage, so generally only the two aforementioned signals need to be simulated. The testing principle for pressure switches is essentially the same as that for flow switches.

For the control valve tamper switch, the testing method is as follows: First, open the valve cover to trigger a trouble signal. Then, manually closing the valve on-site will generate a supervisory signal, indicating that the valve has been manually closed. This signal will be transmitted to the fire alarm control panel.

Testing for generator trouble is relatively simple: Extract the trouble signal from the generator control panel and transmit it to the fire alarm control panel via the fire alarm input circuit to display the generator trouble status.

Testing for generator trouble is relatively simple: Extract the trouble signal from the generator control panel and transmit it to the fire alarm control panel via the fire alarm input circuit to display the generator trouble status.

The above describes the testing methods for initiating devices. Next, we will introduce signaling/notification devices and the test procedure. Taking the red strobe light as an example, its testing method is as follows:

You can use the lighting meter I mentioned earlier for testing. For bells and horns, a signal meter can be used to measure their sound pressure levels.

Typically, the signal meter reading in an office environment ranges from 40 to 50 decibels (dB), while the sound pressure level of fire alarm bells or horns can reach 85 to 95 dB. According to regulatory requirements, as long as the reading is 17 dB above the ambient noise level, it is considered compliant.

This is a fireproof rolling shutter. In the event of a fire, the shutter will descend to isolate two different directional zones. It involves some relays and controllers from the fire alarm system. The controller itself is also equipped with a switch that triggers linkage when the fireproof shutter descends. This is a fire isolation system.

Next is the electromagnetic door release device—what is its function?

This photo shows the status of the door.

Under normal circumstances, the door remains open because it employs a magnetic lock design, which uses an electromagnet to maintain the open position.

In the event of a fire, since these two areas belong to different fire compartments, the fire alarm control panel will send a signal to release the magnetic lock, causing the door to close automatically.

In the event of a fire, since these two areas belong to different fire compartments, the fire alarm control panel will send a signal to release the magnetic lock, causing the door to close automatically.

As you can see, the door is equipped with a closer, so without the magnetic force, the door would automatically shut.

This is the magnetic door release device.

Next, we will discuss the coordinated control of large-scale equipment, such as air conditioning systems. In the event of a fire, the relevant AHUs (Air Handling Units), supply fans, and exhaust fans need to shut down. Additionally, upon fire signal activation, elevators will execute a recall procedure, returning to the main floor; if a fire is detected on the main floor, they will proceed to a designated alternate floor, as programmed by the fire alarm system.

Some clients require the fire alarm signal to be transmitted to the Building Automation System (BAS), enabling the system to receive an alert signal during a fire incident. This design aims to achieve more efficient building safety management.

Typically, a duty officer is stationed inside the building, working from the BAS control room. In the event of a fire, if the fire alarm system sends a signal to the BAS, the on-duty technician will be immediately notified. This functionality relies on the relay connection between the BAS system and the fire alarm system. The fire alarm system transmits output signals to the DDC system, which, upon receiving the signals, displays the fire alarm information on the BAS graphical interface.

This is the communication conduit for the fire alarm control panel, located on its left side.

This is the fire alarm control panel, and this conduit connects to third-party devices. In fact, it employs two distinct communication methods: one is wireless network, and the other is radio. These two methods serve as redundancy for each other.

This is the fire alarm control panel, and this conduit connects to third-party devices. In fact, it employs two distinct communication methods: one is wireless network, and the other is radio. These two methods serve as redundancy for each other.

Normally, the system transmits three types of signals: fire alarm signals, fault signals, and supervisory signals. Fault signals indicate that certain devices in the system have issues or have stopped working; fire signals are well-known; supervisory signals are generated when control valves are closed.

These three types of signals can be received by third-party monitoring companies, which generate reports using the aforementioned two communication methods.

The communication between the Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACP) and the fire alarm annunciator is internal to the fire alarm system, which typically requires minimal debugging.

The communication between the Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACP) and the fire alarm annunciator is internal to the fire alarm system, which typically requires minimal debugging.

The interaction and linkage mechanism of the entire system are as follows: In the event of a fire, the system will activate the corresponding equipment according to the preset procedures.

First, the notification devices need to be activated. These devices include alarms, buzzers, and speakers, among others. Subsequently, the fire alarm control panel will immediately send a signal to the fire department, a process completed through a third-party monitoring company.

Additionally, the sprinkler system will begin operation. When a fire occurs, the glass bulb in the sprinkler head will melt due to high temperatures, releasing water flow. If a fire pump is installed, it will automatically start due to the drop in pipeline pressure.

In high-rise building systems, more complex integrated control solutions must also be considered.

The fire alarm system must activate relevant devices in the event of a fire, including fire dampers and elevator recall. Upon fire detection, elevators will return to the main floor; if the main floor is affected by fire, they will proceed to an alternate floor. Additionally, the system needs to release magnetic doors or close fire doors. The above describes only typical primary联动 functions and is presented here as a brief overview.

Next, we will introduce the technical documentation for the commissioning of the fire alarm system. Regarding this part, I have already mentioned it in the previous two issues of “Building Commissioning Oral Records,” so I will briefly explain it here. These documents include the commissioning report.

I mainly want to share with everyone the Commissioning Report that needs to be filled out during the debugging process, which is a critical step, such as the commissioning report for the Pool Station.

Some forms contain connection information for the Fire Alarm Control Panel, such as the connected Fire Alarm Control Panel, Fire Zone, device number, location, model, etc. Additionally, it is necessary to check whether the Zone Number and Tech Number are appropriate and whether the installation height meets the requirements.

Has Condway been installed? Is the Warning functioning normally? Are there any issues with Pool and Terminate? Are there any defects?

These items belong to the Installation Startup Checklist, which are the items that need to be confirmed before testing and debugging.

Before debugging, it is necessary to inspect the installation status. For the Fire Alarm System, its startup process is relatively simple, mainly involving the inspection of the Fire Alarm Control Panel. A Checklist has been prepared for this purpose.

This is relatively simple; it’s the installation startup checklist.

This is a performance verification checklist applicable to various types of fire alarm equipment. Each device is preceded by testing procedures, which correspond to the content previously outlined.

The first half of the checklist covers basic information, while the latter half pertains to performance testing. For instance, whether a manual call point sends signals to the fire alarm control panel upon being triggered.

Next is the Integrated System Testing Procedure, which involves interoperability testing between systems. This test includes various interoperability scenarios, and the specific interoperability content and main operation sequences should be recorded in a table.

Regarding the sample of Fire Alarm System Commissioning Deliverable, it primarily includes the following items: Commissioning Plan, Commissioning Manual, and Commissioning Report. Additionally, the Issue Log is also quite important, functioning similarly to a common Deficiency List, all of which are typical documents.
